investigacion.base:
**Bottom line:** As of October 19, 2026, the figure is **300**, which would resolve **NO**. A YES needs at least one more history.md entry with a numerator of 301 or higher before October 29 (UTC). The last two entries show no increase.

**What the sources say right now**
- **history.md:** The October 7 entry (committed October 8) says OpenAI added an additional 6 formalizations and 5 other additions covering supporting results, bringing the ratio to 300 / 719, about 42%. The question says there's also an October 13 entry with the same "300 / 719 = ~42%." I couldn't see that entry myself, but secondary sources agree: as of October 13, 2026, the README describes 719 manuscripts in 372 families and approximately 42% of top-line results formalized in Lean.
- **README:** "The repository has ~42% top-line results formalized." It also says "We will continue to update this repository with Lean formalizations as we obtain them."

**Timeline**
- **October 6:** OpenAI released 722 manuscripts in 372 result families.
- **October 7:** Three manuscripts were withdrawn over a sign error, leaving 719. None of the three had Lean formalizations, so the numerator didn't drop. None of the three appear in the Lean catalogue.
- **October 8:** The specific "~42%" sentence first appeared in the README, replacing a much vaguer « Many, but not all, of the manuscripts have been formalized. »
- **October 13:** The numerator was still 300. Revisions continued, but no new formalizations were counted.
- **October 15:** OpenAI's blog post added an "Update, October 15, 2026" about supporting the math community. I couldn't confirm that it changed the count.
- Dan Roberts (OpenAI) said they will 'continue to update the repo with new formalizations and with any errata we notice.'

**Things to weigh**
- **Update pace:** There have been two entries in about a week (October 7 and 13). If that holds, one or two more entries are plausible before October 29. But the only increase so far was +6, at launch. Between October 7 and 13 the count didn't move.
- **The 300 is unexplained:** Independent analyses say the numerator "matches the length of no list this file holds". The catalogue shows 173 of 719 manuscripts (24%) or 135 of 372 families (36%). So it's unclear how new formalizations feed into the headline number, and OpenAI might simply not re-report it.
- **Further withdrawals:** These would push the count down only if a withdrawn result was formalized. All three so far were unformalized. Any decrease resolves NO.
- **Pressure on Lean quality:** Science reports a preprint found that the Lean formalization of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result doesn't match the proof described in the accompanying paper. That could prompt either more formalization work or corrections.

**Base rate:** Only one of two history entries raised the numerator so far. No scheduled events are known before October 29.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any for this question.

criterios: This question resolves YES if, when the openai/math repository's history log at https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/history.md is read on October 29, 2026 (UTC), the most recent entry reports more than 300 top-line results formalized in Lean. The relevant figure is the numerator of the "total percentage of top-line results formalized" fraction in the most recent history entry (for example, the October 13, 2026 entry states "300 / 719 = ~42%", a numerator of 300, which would resolve NO). If the most recent entry instead reports a cumulative count of top-line results formalized, that count is used. The question resolves NO if that figure is 300 or fewer.
letra_pequena: If history.md does not state an explicit numerator but the repository's main README (https://github.com/openai/math) states a percentage of top-line results formalized, the figure is that percentage multiplied by the total number of top-line results the repository states at that time (currently 719), rounded to the nearest whole number. A decrease in the reported figure (for example from further manuscript withdrawals) resolves NO. If the openai/math repository and its history log are permanently unavailable on October 29, 2026, the question is annulled. Only the value as reported on October 29, 2026 (UTC) is used.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About 10 days, from October 19 to the October 29 UTC check.

(b) **Status quo:** NO. The reported numerator is 300.

(c) **Reference class:** For a newly published research repository with few commits and no promised update schedule, I would treat a count-changing update within ten days as a minority outcome—roughly a 25–40% heuristic, not a measured base rate. OpenAI’s stated intention to add formalizations raises the chance, but the recent unchanged count limits it.

(d) **NO scenario:** The repository receives no further update, or an update leaves the reported numerator at 300.

(e) **YES scenario:** OpenAI posts another history entry reporting at least 301 top-line results formalized.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** The *reported figure in the most recent history entry* controls, not the number one might independently count in the repository. If the specified README-percentage fallback applies, “~42%” multiplied by 719 rounds to **302**, which would resolve YES despite no explicitly reported increase.

I put somewhat more weight on NO: the jump to 300 looks like a backfill, and subsequent activity has not raised the headline count.

Probability: 36%

(a) About 10 days remain: the history log is read on October 29, 2026 (UTC), and today is October 19.

(b) If nothing changes, the latest history entry still reads "300 / 719 = ~42%", a numerator of 300. That resolves NO.

(c) Reference class: post-launch update cadence of corporate research repos that promise to add more results "as we obtain them."
- Such repos usually get a burst of updates in the first week or two, then go quiet for long stretches.
- Here the burst already happened: 162 → 300 by about October 7–8.
- The count then held at 300 through October 13.
- There have been no commits since October 12, and only five commits in total.
- The chance of a further increment within a given 10-day window after the initial burst is perhaps 20–35%.

(d) NO scenario: OpenAI's team moves on or works on errata and responses to criticism, such as the Navier-Stokes Lean faithfulness issue. Any further formalizations are held for a larger batched update in November or later, or not re-reported in the headline fraction. Alternatively, an errata-only entry is added with no new numerator, or a withdrawal lowers the count.

(e) YES scenario: OpenAI's internal autoformalization pipeline keeps producing Lean proofs. To answer public scrutiny about the "42%," they push a batch before late October, with a new history entry such as "315 / 719 = ~44%."

(f) Technicalities that could decide it:
- The figure is the numerator in the most recent history entry. An entry with no numerator falls back to the README percentage times 719, so "~42%" maps to about 302.
- Strictly, 0.42 × 719 = 301.98, which rounds to 302 and exceeds 300. That could resolve YES on a technicality even with no new formalizations.
- This fallback only applies if the most recent history entry lacks an explicit numerator. Currently the latest entry states 300 explicitly, so the fallback matters only if a new entry without a numerator gets added.
- Even then, a resolver would likely read "~42%" as consistent with 300, but the ambiguity adds a little YES probability.
- Any decrease resolves NO.

Overall, the status quo of no movement since October 7–8 is weighted heavily, but OpenAI's stated commitment to keep adding formalizations, plus the active scrutiny, leaves a meaningful chance of an update.

Probability: 27%

- **Time left:** About 10 days, until October 29 (UTC).
- **Status quo:** NO. The latest reported numerator is 300.
- **Reference class:** Of the two early history updates, one raised the count and one did not. That 1-in-2 rate is a very small, launch-skewed sample; the lack of a committed update schedule makes it weak evidence for the next ten days.
- **NO scenario:** No new top-line formalizations are reported in the latest history entry by October 29, even if other repository work continues.
- **YES scenario:** A new history entry reports at least 301 top-line results formalized.
- **Resolution technicality:** An explicit numerator in the latest history entry controls. Only if the history log lacks one does the README percentage fallback apply; “~42%” of 719 would round to **302**, despite being consistent with the currently reported 300.

The promised updates make a further increase plausible, but the unchanged recent count and short window favor NO.

Probability: 30%
